In this chapter and the next, we'll cover the techniques of correlation and regression. Whereas the $z$, $t$, and ANOVA statistics we've covered so far deal with examining differences between means, correlation and regression focus on associations between variables. As we'll see, though, this isn't as big a difference as you might expect. Correlation and regression are just another extension of the basic idea of variability that have powered all of our inferential statistics so far.

## Buying happiness

In Chapter 12, we imagined giving people $10 and telling them to spend it either on themselves or on someone else. I based that idea on a real experiment, in which people randomly assigned to spend a small amount of cash on someone else reported being happier later that day than people assigned to spend it on themselves [@dunn2008spending]. At the end of the chapter I made a big to-do about how one study is never the final word on anything.

Well, the researchers actually did more than one kind of study. In the same paper, they reported another in which they didn't give out cash or assign anyone to anything. Instead they just surveyed a representative sample of 632 Americans, asking how happy they were in general and how much they spent in a typical month on gifts for other people and donations to charity.

How might we analyze the data to see whether spending on others goes with being happier? We don't really have groups to compare in this case, just two answers from each person. I suppose we could *make* some groups. We could split the sample into people who spent something on others and people who spent nothing, and compare the two groups' mean happiness with an independent-samples $t$ test.

But that would throw away a lot of good information. Everyone who spent anything gets lumped together, so we lose any distinction between someone who spent $5 on others and someone who spent $500. There has to be a better way! How might we make use of each person's actual amount spent?

::: {#quiz-correlation-pairs}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-pairs.qmd >}}
:::

The idea @quiz-correlation-pairs was getting at is to look at each person's answers together, not to find a difference between them (like the related-samples $t$ test did), but to find an association. Take someone who spent more than average on other people. If that person was also happier than average, their two deviations point in the same direction. How about someone who was both a miser and miserable?^[Yeah, I just figured out those words are related.] Their deviations point in the same direction too.

Here's what that idea looks like with some data. (These aren't the real survey responses, just a handful of made-up people to illustrate.)

::::: {#act-same-side .callout-tip .interactive}

Counting dots in the four sections like this is a rough version of what a correlation does. The real math also takes into account precisely how far each person is from the two means, so that someone far above average on both counts for more than someone only just above. And just as with a difference between group means, we'll need to know whether an apparent pattern is more than we'd expect by chance.

### What would it mean?

Now I know you're excited to do the math, and we'll get to it soon. But first, let's distinguish two closely related terms. A **correlation coefficient** is the number we'll calculate to quantify how two variables go together. **Correlational** also describes a research design. If the researchers had created two groups by letting people choose to spend $10 on themselves or someone else, instead of randomly assigning them, they could have analyzed the data using a $t$ test rather than a correlation coefficient. But it would be a correlational design nonetheless. If the people who spent their money on someone else were happier, would that tell us the same thing as finding that people randomly assigned to do so were happier?

::: {#quiz-correlation-designs}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-designs.qmd >}}
:::

In the actual survey, people who spent more on others did tend to be happier. Can we conclude that spending on others makes people happier? Not necessarily. Maybe being happier makes people more generous. Or maybe there's some other explanation. Perhaps people with higher incomes could afford to give more and also tended to be happier. The researchers anticipated that possibility and asked about income, too. Taking it into account barely changed the association.[^dunn-regression]

[^dunn-regression]: They did this with regression, the topic of the next chapter.

That rules out one alternative explanation, but I'm sure you can think of others. The researchers hadn't measured everything that might make people both more generous and happier. As Dunn and colleagues put it themselves, "the correlational nature of this design precludes causal inferences."

That's why they did the experiment, giving people some money and telling them who to spend it on. But experiments have disadvantages of their own. In everyday life, people aren't usually handed an envelope of cash and told how to spend it. An experiment can give a causal answer to a narrow, somewhat contrived question. The survey answers a more realistic question, less conclusively. Together they contribute to a body of evidence, but neither is definitive on its own.

## The correlation coefficient

Now we can get into the details of the correlation statistic itself. The statistic we'll use is called **Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient**, named after Karl Pearson---the statistician Gosset went to study with in Chapter 11. But its development also involved another familiar figure: Francis Galton, whose board of bouncing balls helped us think about sampling in Chapter 7.

Galton was interested in how people's physical characteristics varied together. Taller people tend to have bigger feet, for example, but not always. How could you put a number on the consistency of the relationship between measurements? Galton had already used the letter $r$ in his work on regression, the closely related technique we'll meet in the next chapter. But Pearson developed the mathematical treatment behind the coefficient we use today [@pearson1896regression], which is why it bears his name.

### Characteristics

The correlation coefficient is a single number that quantifies the **strength** and **direction** of a linear association between two quantitative variables.[^other-correlations] Because of how it's calculated, $r$ can range from $-1$ to $1$.

[^other-correlations]: The same calculation turns up under a few other names. Pearson's $r$ calculated on ranks is *Spearman's rank correlation*. If one variable is quantitative and the other is coded 0 or 1, it's a *point-biserial correlation*. Coding the two spending groups in Chapter 12 that way gives $r = .28$ (with spend-on-other coded 1), and testing it gives the same $t(8) = 0.82$ we got by comparing means. If both variables are coded 0 or 1, the correlation is called *phi*.

The absolute value quantifies the strength of the relationship, or, in other words, the consistency of the association between the variables. The stronger and more consistent their association, the closer the correlation will be to 1 (or $-1$). The weaker and less consistent their relationship, the closer the correlation will be to 0.

The sign, positive or negative, indicates the direction of the correlation. A positive correlation is one for which increases in one variable are associated with increases in the other---or, correspondingly, lower scores on one are associated with lower scores on the other. A negative correlation means that higher scores on one variable are associated with lower scores on the other---that they move in opposite directions.

These characteristics are illustrated in the scatterplots in @fig-cor-characteristics.

:::: {#fig-cor-characteristics}

Scatterplots illustrating various correlation coefficients. I've drawn an ellipse to summarize the shape of the cloud. The stronger the correlation, the closer the cloud comes to forming a straight line.
::::

At zero, the ellipse in @fig-cor-characteristics is basically a circle, with no upward or downward tendency, meaning that there is no consistent linear relationship between the two variables. As the correlation gets stronger, the ellipse gets longer and thinner. A "perfect correlation" of either $1$ or $-1$ means that every change in one variable is accompanied by a proportional change in the other; the dots fall into a straight line, and the ellipse becomes a line. In a sense, the correlation coefficient is a measure of how closely the data points follow a straight-line pattern.[^scatterplot-scale-note]

[^scatterplot-scale-note]: I should note that changing the scale of one axis doesn't change the correlation, but it can make the ellipse look more or less rotund. The correlation coefficient measures how consistently the two variables go together, relative to their separate variability, rather than how the pattern happens to look in a particular graph with its particular scales and dimensions.

## Calculating $r$

Now let's see how to calculate Pearson's $r$. It's based on the ideas of **variability** and **covariability**.

Here's the equation for Pearson's $r$:

$$ r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} $$ {#eq-pearson-r}

$SS_X$ and $SS_Y$ should look familiar. $SS$, as usual, refers to the sum of squared deviations, a measure of how scores vary around their mean. So here we have the separate sums of squares for $X$ and $Y$ getting combined in the denominator.

The numerator is a new quantity, $SP$, the **sum of products**. This quantifies the *covariability* of $X$ and $Y$: the extent to which changes in $X$ are associated with corresponding changes in $Y$.

Remember that to calculate $SS$, we square the deviation scores. And another way of saying that we square something is to say we multiply it by itself. So here are two equivalent ways of writing the equation for sum of squares:

$$ SS = \Sigma(X - M)^2 $$

$$ SS = \Sigma(X - M)(X - M) $$

The reason I point this out is that $SP$ does something quite similar, but instead of multiplying deviations by *themselves*, like $SS$ does, we multiply them by *one another*, to get the product of the two deviations. Then we sum those products to get the sum of products, $SP$.

$$ SP = \Sigma(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y) $$ {#eq-sum-of-products}

With $SS$ we ask how far the scores on one variable spread around their mean. With $SP$ we get to keep the signs of the products. Above average on both? Positive. Below average on both? Also positive. Above on one and below on the other? That will make for a negative product. While $SS$ can only be positive, $SP$ can be positive or negative, depending on whether the two variables tend to go together or in opposite directions.

### Worked example

Let's work through a simple example to see how the sum of products is calculated. Suppose we're interested in how the number of cups of coffee a student drinks on the morning of a test is related to their score. Maybe the caffeine will increase alertness and cognitive performance, leading to better test scores. We have data for seven students, as shown in @tbl-coffee-scores.

| Participant | Coffee (cups), $X$ | Test score, $Y$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 75 |

: Cups of coffee and test scores for seven students. {#tbl-coffee-scores}

Before we work through the full calculation, let's picture the two sums of squares and the sum of products for this little dataset.

Each student has two deviations: how far they are from the mean on $X$, and how far they are from the mean on $Y$. Student A drank 1 cup less than average and scored 20 points above average. Student G is above average on both.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Products" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":true,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Now we multiply each student's two deviations. The product is the area of the resulting rectangle, one deviation wide and the other deviation tall. The dots labeled A, C, E, and F are above one mean and below the other, so their deviations have opposite signs and their products are negative. Those are the orange rectangles with dashed outlines. Points B and G are on the same side of both means, so their products are positive. D is exactly at the mean for coffee, so its product is zero.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="$SP$" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":true,"show-sp":true,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Add up the products and we have the sum of products: $SP = -20 + 5 - 7.5 + 0 - 10 - 2.5 + 5 = -30$. The negative products outweigh the positive ones, so $SP$ comes out negative.
:::
::::

:::::

If you're working by hand, @tbl-r-definitional is Chapter 4's deviations table extended to include deviations and squared deviations for both variables. There's just one new column, for those products. To make it, we multiply each row's two deviations to get the product, then sum up that column to get $SP$.

| $X$ | $X - M_X$ | $(X - M_X)^2$ | $Y$ | $Y - M_Y$ | $(Y - M_Y)^2$ | $(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y)$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | $-1$ | 1 | 90 | 20 | 400 | $-20$ |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 60 | $-10$ | 100 | 5 |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 85 | 15 | 225 | $-7.5$ |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | 0 |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 50 | $-20$ | 400 | $-10$ |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | $-2.5$ |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 75 | 5 | 25 | 5 |
| | | $SS_X = 3$ | | | $SS_Y = 1200$ | $SP = -30$ |

: Deviations, squared deviations, and products for the coffee data. $M_X = 1$; $M_Y = 70$. {#tbl-r-definitional}

That gives us everything we need to calculate the correlation coefficient:

$$r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} = \frac{-30}{\sqrt{3 \times 1200}} = \frac{-30}{60} = -.50$$

<!-- Notice what the denominator is doing there. Our sum of products came out at $-30$, and the denominator at 60. Now imagine the same amount of variability on each variable, but with every student falling exactly on a straight line. Then every change in $X$ would be accompanied by a proportional change in $Y$, and the covariability in the numerator would be as big in magnitude as their separate variabilities combined in the denominator. $SP$ would be $-60$, and $r$ would be $-1$. In other words, all the variability would be covariability, just as we saw when the ellipse collapsed into a line. There'd be no variability that isn't shared. The more unshared variability there is, the closer the correlation coefficient gets to zero. When there is no shared linear variability at all, the numerator will be zero, and so will the correlation coefficient. This is why $r$ can only vary between negative one and positive one. -->

::: {#quiz-correlation-calculate-r}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-calculate-r.qmd >}}
:::

## A correlation test, step by step

So we've calculated a correlation coefficient, $r$, for our little coffee consumption and test performance data set. The correlation came out negative: drinking more coffee was associated with lower test scores. But is that a significant relationship, or just due to chance? To know that, we need to submit the data to a full hypothesis test, following the same basic procedure we've used for every other hypothesis test.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

We use $r$ for the sample correlation and the Greek letter $\rho$ (rho) for the population correlation. The null hypothesis sets $\rho$ to zero. Our nondirectional alternative allows for a linear association in either direction.

$$ H_0: \rho = 0 $$

$$ H_1: \rho \ne 0 $$

So the correlation hypothesis test asks, how likely is it that a correlation as strong as the one we observed would occur if there were no association in the population?

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

This is going to sound weird, but the test statistic for a correlation is actually a $t$ statistic. Pearson's $r$ describes the size of the association in our sample, not how probable it is under the null hypothesis. So to test the null, we turn the $r$ into a $t$. We'll see how in the next step, but for now, we need its degrees of freedom to find the critical $t$. Its degrees of freedom are $n - 2$, where $n$ counts the pairs. Seven students give us seven observations of the relationship, even though we've recorded fourteen scores.

Why subtract two? Well, picture what would happen with just two points on a scatterplot. We could always draw a straight line passing through both, fitting perfectly. The correlation would be one or negative one. There'd be no opportunity for either point to deviate from the line, because those two points determine the line itself. It's only when we add more observations that we can see any scatter around it. So fitting the line uses up two degrees of freedom, leaving $n - 2$ deviations free to vary.^[Slightly more technically, we're estimating the slope and intercept of the line from the data, and each estimated parameter costs a degree of freedom. We'll go into more detail on that in the next chapter.]

So with seven pairs of scores in our data set, we have $df = 5$. For our two-tailed test at $\alpha = .05$, the critical values are $\pm 2.571$.

::: {#tbl-correlation-critical}
{{< interactive-figure correlationCriticalTable makeTTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the coffee test","df":{"from":1,"to":7},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","confidence":false,"interactive":false,"selected":{"df":5,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05}}' fallback="t table excerpt for 1 through 7 degrees of freedom, highlighting the two-tailed .05 critical value of 2.571 at df = 5." >}}

An excerpt of the $t$ table, with the $df = 5$ row highlighted. The two-tailed $.05$ heading puts $.025$ in each tail.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

We already found $r = -.50$ (@tbl-r-definitional). Now we need to convert that into a $t$ statistic. Remember the basic structure of a $t$ statistic (@eq-t-structure)? We subtract a population parameter defined by the null hypothesis from our sample statistic, then divide by a standard error. Here the null says $\rho = 0$, and our sample statistic is $r$. The denominator is the standard error of the correlation, $s_r$.

$$ t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} $$ {#eq-correlation-t}

The equation for the standard error of the correlation is a little different from the ones we've seen before. It depends on the correlation itself, as well as the number of pairs of scores.

$$ s_r = \sqrt{\frac{1 - r^2}{n - 2}} $$ {#eq-correlation-se}

Remember how $\eta^2$ in Chapter 14 told us what proportion of the total variability was accounted for by differences between the groups? $r^2$ does a similar job for a linear relationship: it tells us the proportion of the variability in one variable that's shared with the other. For our coffee data, $r^2 = (-.50)^2 = .25$. So 25% of the variability in test scores is shared with coffee consumption, leaving 75% unaccounted for by that relationship. In terms of the scatterplot, that's the variability in the points above and below the regression line. That's the $1 - r^2$ in the numerator.

So the standard error reflects variability left over after accounting for the predictable relationship, divided by the degrees of freedom, with a square root to undo the squaring. A stronger correlation makes the standard error smaller, becuase there is more predictability, less variability unaccounted for. As with the other standard errors we've seen, more observations make it smaller too, because more data gives us a more precise estimate.

For our coffee data, that works out like this:

$$t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} = \frac{-.50 - 0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - (-.50)^2}{7 - 2}}} = \frac{-.50}{.387} = -1.29$$

### Step 4: Make a decision

Our $t = -1.29$ falls between the two critical values, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

::: {#fig-correlation-decision}
{{< interactive-figure correlationTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"t","df":5,"title":"Null distribution: df = 5","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[-5,5],"xTicks":5,"labels":{"x":"t statistic"},"shade":{"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":-2.570582,"label":"−2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.570582,"label":"+2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":-1.290994,"label":"t = −1.29","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom. The two rejection regions lie beyond ±2.571; the observed t of −1.29 falls between them." >}}

The observed $t = -1.29$ falls between the critical values of the null $t$ distribution with $df = 5$.
:::

The corresponding two-tailed $p$-value is approximately $.25$, well above our $\alpha$ of $.05$.

## Reporting and interpreting the results

### Reporting results

As always, we need to report the results of our hypothesis test. Here, that statement will include the value of the correlation coefficient, Pearson's $r$, its degrees of freedom, and the $p$-value for the correlation.

> Drinking more coffee was associated with lower test scores, but the correlation did not reach statistical significance; $r(5) = -.50$, $p = .25$.

### Interpreting the results

So what can we make of our result? We failed to reject the null hypothesis, but that doesn't establish that there's no relationship. We only have seven pairs of scores. Our $r = -.50$ describes a fairly strong negative association in this sample, but with so few observations, it isn't strong enough evidence to reject the null.

::: {#quiz-correlation-significance}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-significance.qmd >}}
:::

On the other hand, a weak correlation can be statistically significant, if it comes from a large enough sample. Suppose we increased the sample for our study up to $n =  300$. In the larger sample, the correlation between coffee and test score is only $-.15$. This smaller correlation would reach statistical significance, $r(298) = -.15$, $p = .009$. So whether a correlation is significant and how strong it is are separate questions.

That significance decision comes down to a binary threshold, but how should we interpret the correlation as a measure of effect size? How impressive is a correlation of $.15$? What about $.05$, or $.30$? Cohen called $r = .30$ *medium*. Funder and Ozer, whose argument about small effects adding up we met in Chapter 9, call it *large* in psychological research [@funder2019evaluating]. In the social sciences, the behaviors or attitudes or whatever we're interested in are generally multiply determined. There are a lot of reasons why you get a particular score on a particular exam, not just how many cups of coffee you drank or how many hours of sleep you get. Those things might just reveal a small piece of the puzzle. And a small piece can be worth knowing about, even if it doesn't look terribly impressive on a scatterplot (@fig-correlation-effect-sizes).

::::: {#fig-correlation-effect-sizes}
::: {.sfs-figure-row}
{{< interactive-figure correlationEffectSizes05 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.05,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":280,"xDomain":[0,100],"yDomain":[0,100]}' fallback="Scatterplot of 100 observations with r = .05. There is barely any visible pattern; the ellipse is almost a circle." >}}

{{< interactive-figure correlationEffectSizes30 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.3,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":280,"xDomain":[0,100],"yDomain":[0,100]}' fallback="The same 100 observations rearranged to give r = .30. There is a visible upward trend, though scores still vary widely at any given X." >}}
:::
A very small correlation ($r = .05$, left) and a large one by Funder and Ozer's standards ($r = .30$, right). At $.05$ there's barely any visible pattern. At $.30$ there's a more obvious upward trend. It would generally be considered quite a strong relationship in the context of social scientific research, even though there is still a lot of variability around the trend. In the social sciences, there always will be.
:::::

### Correlation and causation

In the spending survey, the researchers asked whether income could account for the relationship between giving and happiness. But what does "taking income into account" actually involve? We can see the basic idea using nothing more than correlations.

Think back to our coffee and test score example. We found a negative correlation between coffee consumption and test scores, but we don't know whether drinking coffee is causing lower test scores, or whether students who expect to do poorly on the exam are drinking more coffee, or whether some other factor is behind both. Maybe students who haven't been sleeping are both drinking more coffee and scoring lower on the exam.

So suppose the study also recorded each student's average nightly sleep over the week before the exam. (That sleep came before the morning's coffee, so the coffee can't have caused it.) Here are our seven students again, with their sleep. (We'll use all 300 students for the correlations, but this shows what the data look like with a third variable.)

| Participant | Coffee (cups) | Test score | Sleep (hours) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 | 9 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 | 8 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 | 8 |
| D | 1 | 65 | 5 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 | 6 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 | 6 |
| G | 2 | 75 | 7 |

: The seven students from @tbl-coffee-scores, now with their average nightly sleep over the week before the exam. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-scores}

With three variables we can calculate three correlations, one for each pair. @tbl-coffee-sleep-correlations shows them for all 300 students in what's called a **correlation matrix**. Pick a row and a column and read across and down to where they meet. We've only filled in the lower half because correlating sleep with coffee gives us exactly the same number as correlating coffee with sleep.

| | Coffee | Test score | Sleep |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Coffee | --- | | |
| Test score | $-.15$ | --- | |
| Sleep | $-.35$ | $.30$ | --- |

: Correlation matrix for coffee, test score, and sleep across all 300 students in the invented study. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-correlations}

Students who slept less tended to drink more coffee ($r = -.35$) and get lower test scores ($r = .30$). So how much of the relationship between coffee and test score is still there once we take sleep into account?

We can work that out with a **partial correlation**. Think of two students who got the same amount of sleep. Would knowing which one drank more coffee still tell us anything about who scored higher? For each student, we work out how much more or less coffee they drank than we'd predict from their sleep using a straight line. Then we do the same for their test score. The partial correlation is the correlation between those two sets of deviations. We can calculate it directly from the three correlations in the table. Here $X$ is coffee, $Y$ is test score, and $Z$ is sleep.

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{r_{XY} - r_{XZ}\,r_{YZ}}{\sqrt{(1 - r_{XZ}^2)(1 - r_{YZ}^2)}} $$ {#eq-partial-r}

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{-.15 - (-.35)(.30)}{\sqrt{(1 - (-.35)^2)(1 - .30^2)}} = \frac{-.045}{.894} = -.05 $$

::: {#fig-coffee-test-third-variable}

{{< include resources/figures/coffee-test-third-variable.svg >}}

Accounting for sleep. The solid lines show sleep's correlations with coffee and with test score. The dashed line shows the correlation between coffee and test score that remains after accounting for sleep: $-.05$, down from $-.15$. All values are invented.

:::

Accounting for sleep brings the correlation much closer to zero, from $-.15$ to $-.05$. Compare that with the spending survey at the beginning of the chapter. There, taking income into account barely changed the association between spending on others and happiness.

::: {#quiz-correlation-partial}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-partial.qmd >}}
:::

For the full sample of 300, the partial correlation falls short of statistical significance, $t(297) = -0.87$, $p = .39$. (We lose one more degree of freedom for each variable we account for, so here $df = n - 3$.) But we can see how much the association shrank by comparing the two coefficients themselves. Crossing the $.05$ threshold doesn't tell us how much anything changed.

Does that settle what caused the lower scores? Even if these were real students, we'd only have accounted for the sleep we measured. Other differences between students could still be involved. That's the advantage of random assignment back in Chapter 12. It gives even the differences we didn't think to measure the same distribution across groups on average. What lets us draw a causal conclusion is how the study was done. Running a $t$ test on groups the students chose for themselves wouldn't turn our survey into an experiment.

::: {#quiz-correlation-causation}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-your-turn-causation.qmd >}}
:::

### Correlation assumptions

With correlational data, we have pairs of scores from the same person; obviously, the pairs aren't independent. As with the related-samples analyses we've used where this was also the case, the assumption of **independence** applies *between* people.

Pearson's correlation also assumes the pairs of scores come from a **bivariate normal distribution**. With the $t$ test and ANOVA we've assumed that the populations that produced samples of scores are normally distributed. With our paired correlational data, the assumption is that both populations---the population of $X$ scores and the population of $Y$ scores---are normally distributed together. Visually, the cloud of dots on a scatterplot should be densest in the middle and thinning out smoothly toward the edges, both horizontally and vertically (@fig-bivariate-normality). The test can tolerate some departures from bivariate normality, though seven pairs tell us little about the shape of the population.

The points are densest in the middle and thin out evenly in every direction." >}}

Two clouds of 100 points with the same correlation, $r = .50$. On the left, the points come from a bivariate normal distribution: densest in the middle and thinning out evenly in every direction. On the right, both variables are positively skewed. The points pile up in the lower-left corner and straggle out to the upper right, violating the assumption.
::::

Lastly, when I defined Pearson's $r$, I said it measures the strenght of *linear* association: how consistently the points follow a straight line. So if we calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient, we're assuming **linearity**.

But things can also be related in ways that a straight line doesn't capture. Maybe the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ starts out with $Y$ increases as $X$ increases, but changes direction at some point; as $X$ keeps increasing $Y$ starts to decrease. (The first scoop of ice cream might improve your mood; by the fourth you might start feeling worse.) Or maybe $X$ and $Y$ keep increasing together, but the rate of increase changes at some point. @fig-scatter-nonlinear illustrates some predictable (though increasingly contrived) relationships that Pearson's $r$ fails to capture. This is why it's worth looking at the scatterplot before trying to summarize the relationship with a single number.
